analysis.one_liner: Lets pharmacists automatically substitute any FDA-licensed biosimilar for its brand-name biologic.
analysis.headline: The Senate health committee reported the bill favorably in July 2026 with bipartisan sponsorship, and it now sits on the Senate calendar waiting for a floor vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current law, a copy of a brand-name biologic drug (called a biosimilar) must clear extra FDA requirements before it can be automatically swapped for the original at the pharmacy. This bill scraps those extra steps: every biosimilar the FDA licenses would be deemed interchangeable the moment it is approved, so pharmacists could substitute it for the pricier original under state law. It preserves the exclusivity rewards already promised to the first interchangeable biosimilars licensed before the change.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who take expensive biologic drugs, such as those for arthritis, cancer, diabetes, and autoimmune disease. Making every licensed biosimilar interchangeable lets pharmacists substitute the cheaper copy without the patient or prescriber doing anything extra, depending on state law [S2]. It also speeds biosimilar makers to market by deleting a separate FDA review track [S2].

how_it_helps.text: The bill eliminates the additional FDA requirements for demonstrating interchangeability, deeming all licensed biosimilars interchangeable with their reference products, so pharmacists can substitute them when filling prescriptions under state law [S2].
New biosimilars would be deemed interchangeable upon licensure, and previously licensed ones 60 days after enactment, removing a slower, separate approval track [S2] [S3].
The bill preserves the marketing exclusivity period for the first interchangeable biosimilars licensed before enactment, so existing exclusivity deals are not wiped out [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name biologic manufacturers, who currently face an extra barrier protecting them from automatic pharmacy substitution. Every licensed biosimilar becoming interchangeable erodes the premium pricing their patents and the interchangeability rules protect. Taxpayers and insurers who cover these drugs are second-order beneficiaries, not payers.

drawbacks.text: The bill removes the FDA's case-by-case judgment that a specific biosimilar is safe to switch; products deemed interchangeable would no longer need to demonstrate switching safety through those additional requirements [S2]. FDA draft guidance in 2024 had already proposed making some of these requirements, including switching-safety studies, optional, but that guidance was never finalized [S2].
Actual substitution still depends on state pharmacy law, so patients in states that do not allow substitution gain less [S2].

Newer biosimilars that rely on the same reference product as an existing one with an unexpired first-interchangeable exclusivity period must wait until that exclusivity ends before being deemed interchangeable, slowing competition for some drugs [S2] [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill trades the FDA's individualized switching-safety review for broader, faster substitution. That review was a meaningful safeguard, but the FDA itself had proposed loosening parts of it, and biosimilars still must pass a full biosimilarity review before licensure [S2]. The main cost is borne by brand-name drug makers, not patients, and the main gain — easier access to cheaper copies of very expensive drugs — goes to patients and payers. The grandfathered exclusivity and state-law limits keep the benefit from being instant or complete.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in June 2025, cleared the Senate health committee on a favorable report in July 2026, and now waits on the Senate calendar for floor time.

narrative.text: Sen. Mike Lee introduced the bill on June 4, 2025, with five cosponsors split between the parties: three Democrats (Luján, Hassan, Ossoff) and two Republicans (Paul, Schmitt) [S3] [S4] [S5].
The Senate referred it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee on the day of introduction [S5].
The committee ordered the bill reported favorably with a substitute amendment on June 17, 2026, and Senator Cassidy formally reported it on July 27, 2026 [S5].

The reported version was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders (Calendar No. 521) on July 27, 2026, meaning it is eligible for floor consideration but has not been scheduled for a vote [S3] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, biosimilar makers and backers of cheaper copies of brand-name biologics, since the bill cleared committee and is one procedural step from the Senate floor. Nothing is yet law, so no one has fully won or lost.

sides.party_line_note: Five cosponsors split 3 Democrats and 2 Republicans, and the HELP committee reported the bill favorably; no senator is on record in the provided materials opposing it, and no floor vote has been scheduled.

industries.note: Every FDA-licensed biosimilar would be automatically interchangeable, deleting a costly and slow second approval track and opening pharmacy substitution under state law [S2]. Their gain comes from competing on price against the original drugs.

The extra interchangeability requirements currently shield originator biologics from automatic substitution; the bill removes that shield 60 days after enactment [S2] [S3]. Their interest runs against patients seeking cheaper versions of the same drugs.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits on the Senate calendar, which means it can be called up for a vote but most bills at this stage wait indefinitely for floor time. Its bipartisan sponsorship and a favorable committee report improve its odds, but unless leadership schedules it or it attaches to a larger drug-pricing vehicle, it will likely remain on the calendar until the Congress ends.
